utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that our transcriber has no audio or ... apparently he can't hear us, which does not appear on the transcript, of course, then. Can you now hear me? Yes, apparently.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And this all happened after I had invited you to call the case and after we had resolved an audio problem for our transcriber. No preliminaries. Therefore the witness can be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, that is that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Vanderpuye will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, good morning to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Colonel. Let me start by asking you this, Colonel Salapura. When you returned to the -- or, rather, arrived, I should say, at the command post at the VRS on 13 July in the afternoon, did you hear anything further about the prisoners that you'd seen earlier at Nova Kasaba, the football stadium?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear anything over there. I don't think that any of those who were there had any information. During my presence there, we were not receiving any information from the AOR of the Drina Corps. I only found my desk officer for electronic reconnaissance there and a warrant officer who was in charge of the logbook where documents were filed and so on, in my department.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, Colonel, report your observations concerning the prisoners that you had seen earlier that day to anyone at the Main Staff when you returned that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. It was only natural. One operation ended, I saw prisoners standing in the football pitch, just as when I was in Potocari, I saw a relaxed movement, nothing special, and nothing out of the ordinary or not normal. And it is only natural that such a large operation would have so many prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You didn't actually -- let me ask: Did you make arrangements or take any steps to see that those prisoners were interrogated or investigated for the purposes of your intelligence function as a chief of the intelligence administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take any steps. I wasn't able to either. Firstly because this was already in the course of preparations for the operation, the orders and documents of the commanders regulated all these arrangements. I didn't take part in either the planning or the implementation stage of the operation, nor was I authorised to interfere with these affairs. With my departure to Banja Luka for my sick leave and medical treatment, we agreed and General Tolimir took over the duty to coordinate the work of all these organs in the eastern area, whereas I was supposed to monitor the events in the west, as far as I was able to, along with the 410th Intelligence Centre, especially the developments with regard to the aggression by Croatia and their attack on Bosnian Krajina. So those were my assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So the short answer is that you didn't take any steps to see that the prisoners that you had earlier seen in Nova Kasaba were questioned or intelligence obtained from them, is that -- is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't take such steps, nor was I able to, but somebody else probably did. The interrogation of prisoners of war starts from the battalion level and the organs there, and then up to the brigade, and everything else is already done in the POW camps, according to our rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, Colonel. Let me show you P1501. This is a document you've seen before, I'm sure. It's the Zvornik Brigade duty officer notebook. I'd like to take you to page 41 of the English and page 40 in the B/C/S, which reflects an entry on 14 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the Registry, this is the same document, the English is just the next page over, so it will be page 41. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see at the bottom of the page, for you, Colonel, the handwriting in your language, but it reflects the entry: "Colonel Salapura called" --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- "Drago and Beara are to report to Golic." Do you have any further recollection of this particular message than you did the last time you testified?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the second day of my presence there. I don't think that I can possibly remember anything else. Interestingly enough, there is no time indicating when the message was received. I might have received it or probably received it at lunchtime or at dinner time. When Mandic, who was the only officer there, when they went to have their dinner, I was the one who stayed behind and I probably then received the message and conveyed it further. I might have received the message from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, we are interested in what you remember, not in what could possibly, whether it was a lunch, breakfast or dinner, that is all -- these are not facts. These are attempts to explain matters of which you say you have no recollection. Let's stick to the facts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, do you know what Colonel Beara or Major Golic or Drago Nikolic were involved in on the 14th of July, 1995, up in the Zvornik area at least as concerns Drago Nikolic and Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a different service, security service. I really don't know. They were working according to their own plan, according to a plan that I was not involved in. I didn't know what was being done on that day. I did not get involved in the command and control system. I stayed there by happenstance. I was not able to go back to Banja Luka because the road was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you an entry at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read here: "Colonel Salapura called Drago and Beara are to report to Golic," which in my understanding of the English language would mean that it was the Colonel who called, whereas part of his answer seems to be that he received a call. Could we clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I do appreciate that. I hadn't noticed it in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, do you have any recollection of calling the Zvornik Brigade duty officer to leave the message that's indicated here for Drago Nikolic and Colonel Beara to report to Major Golic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall the details, but if I may explain something, Golic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. You are not here to explain unless you explain facts. You say you don't recall the details. What do you recall? If it is -- even if it is without details.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To state the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will explain this fact only without going into detail. Golic was an officer, a Major in the intelligence service. The two mentioned here, Drago Nikolic and Beara, they were in the security service. This term is -- this is an assumption, it's something that was mentioned in the Tolimir case. Not that he should report -- he wouldn't say report to Vlasenica but report to Golic, not to report to Han Pijesak, report to Salapura. So I assume that that that's the same message. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We are not interested in your assumptions at this moment, unless Mr. Vanderpuye asks questions, again we would like to know facts. The book says "Colonel Salapura called," your answer is, "I don't have a recollection that I did." We leave it to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Just so that we are clear, I can't see if it's reflected in there, you don't have a recollection as to what Drago Nikolic and Colonel Beara were doing in the Zvornik area on the 14th of July, 1995, is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It's also true that I didn't have any contact whatsoever in this period with Beara or Drago Nikolic. I didn't see him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is given by "that's right." You are explaining a lot of things. We are interested in what you could tell us about the facts, just that. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go, please, to page 45 in the English and page 44 in the B/C/S of the same exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you should see in your own language, Colonel, is an entry beginning with 1500 hours and it says, "Colonel Beara is coming in order to," and then it says, "Orovac, Petkovci, Rocevic, Pilica." Can you see that entry, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know what that concerns?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know what Colonel Beara was doing in relation to these locations, Orahovac - "Orovac" it says in here but the Chamber has heard evidence that it refers to Orahovac - Petkovci, Rocevic, and Pilica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I think that the witness answered the question in his previous answer. So this is an answered question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said "no," interpreter's note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This question focuses and certain specific locations, but to that extent, it is not exactly the same, but the witness has answered the question and I think we can proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to show you a couple of entries and then I'll turn you over to the Defence. One is at page 54 in the B/C/S, page 55 in the English. Here we can see another reference in the middle of the page to Beara and it says "to call 155." Are you familiar with that extension or that number in the context of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. It's been a long time. I can't remember which number that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you page 78 in the B/C/S and page 79 in the English, see if that helps refresh your recollection. This is an entry on the 16th of July but it refers to, again, 155, you can see at the bottom of the page. And there it says, "Beara to call Panorama 155." Does that help refresh your recollection as to what that number relates to in the context of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you that I did not participate in the planning, and these are code names, so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've given the answer. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you -- you mentioned at the very beginning of your evidence that you learned about the participation of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in the Srebrenica-related executions from its commander Milorad Pelemis. I think you said perhaps late December 1995 or early 1996. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Misstatement. The witness did not say that he learned of the participation of the 10th Sabotage Detachment but, rather, of individual members of that detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you had your conversation with Pelemis, the commander, did he tell you about the involvement of the unit or members of the unit at any of the locations that I just showed you in the duty officer logbook, that is, in relation to Pilica, Rocevic, Petkovci or Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't ask that from him either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you about the involvement of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in the executions at Bisina, near Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in relation to what he told you about participation of members of the unit in the executions related to Srebrenica, did you personally take any action with respect to that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't because this was not my jurisdiction. I think that measures had already been taken, such as investigative measures, but I did not get involved in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You didn't because it was not within your jurisdiction. That's the answer to the question. What you think, whether measures were taken, et cetera, if you're aware of any measures, tell us. But what you think, just as a vague expression of what might have happened, doesn't assist the Chamber. Do you have any specific information about measures taken by others? When, by whom, what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an answer to my question. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In respect of what Pelemis told you concerning the participation of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in these crimes, you did, nevertheless, request that these members be provided with new identifications from the Minister of the Interior, Dragan Kijac, in January of 1996. Was that done on the authorisation of your commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I submitted that request on my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Vanderpuye, could I ask the witness, was that within your jurisdiction to provide others with new identity cards? Was that part of your job? And where is that described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The duties that I was performing, as well as others, included such cases. I think that it was used in many other services across the world. But this had a completely different goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My first question was -- and the reference to the rest of the world is rather vague as a legal basis for providing new IDs. My question was whether it was within your jurisdiction and where that is described. Do you have any text where it says, "In my position I am there to provide new IDs"? Anywhere specific? If not, we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anything specific. If need be I can only explain why I did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vanderpuye, if you're interested to know why the witness did it, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, I think we have that already in your prior evidence, sir. It is fair to say, though, that the eight nationals for which you requested the identification were individuals that you believed had been indicted by The Hague Tribunal and that was one of the reasons that was indicated in the specific request that you made in 16 January 1996 for the issuance of those identifications; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that's what it says, what it says is accurate, but why did I write it, if I can explain?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I've asked you is what I've asked you. If you want to answer a different question, then wait for it to be posed. But I'd like to show this document to you so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's P1586. This is the document that I was referring to. You can see that it's dated -- I see the B/C/S is kind of faint. But we can see the date at the top, 16 January 1996, and the substance of it -- well, it's directed to the Minister of the Interior, to the minister personally, and beneath that it reflects the following: "Considering that we have a group of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment who are foreign citizens or are on a list of individuals who have been indicted by The Hague Tribunal, we ask that you order the Bijeljina MUP to issue personal IDs with Serbian first and last names to these individuals or with different first and last names for Serbian nationals. There are eight such individuals." You wrote this, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it was directed to the Minister of the Interior, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And for you to have done this, it would have been done on the approval of General Tolimir, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most likely there was a reason. Probably Tolimir wasn't there, so I was there in his stead. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. Mr. Stojanovic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, sir, good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll start with the latest question pertaining to the 10th Sabotage Detachment. I wanted to ask you to explain to the Court when it was created.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was in 1994, at least in this form that was later on supplemented. Before the detachment -- sorry, well, the VRS was created on the basis of the 2nd Military District. By the same token, there was the 5th and then the 2nd Sabotage Detachment. It was disbanded because it had suffered significant losses, so it became nearly non-existent. And later on, the other one was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the point, the idea, of establishing such a detachment with the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exclusive task of that detachment was to carry out combat activities in enemy territory, so it included sabotage and reconnaissance activities deep inside enemy territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the make-up, the ethnic make-up, in the detachment? Was it of -- were the members of mixed ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What prompted the VRS to establish a multi-ethnic formation in a unit of this kind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were several circumstances which affected it. There were some members of other ethnicities who volunteered and who had their military specialty from the time when they had served their military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that in the 10th Sabotage Detachment, there were Slovenians, Croats, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war activities ended, did such individuals have problems with the authorities of their own states or entities for their participation in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't go there. They remained in VRS territory or went abroad. However, when they were still there, there was some interest on the part of the AID for the persons in that unit. That was the extent of information we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it for that reason that they asked for their identity to be changed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A change of identity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, we don't have any evidence to the effect that they asked for their identities to be changed. What we have from the exhibit that was shown was that the witness asked their identity to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Then I will lay a foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, were there requests by members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment to have their identities changed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was our assessment that it was necessary to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Kindly tell us, until what time did the unit exist as an autonomous unit of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It existed until after the war, until 1996, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will try to deal briefly with the facts and I'll try to be as focused on that as possible, and I want to go back to your statement and discuss the chronology. To the best of your recollection, on the 12th of July, when did you arrive in Bijeljina attempting to contact the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon my return from Belgrade, which was in the early evening or sometime later in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You were accompanied by two members from your Main Staff organ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us try -- actually, can you explain briefly the composition of the intelligence organ and its composition in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intelligence organ included myself, as the chief of intelligence administration. Then there was the head of the analysis department, who was also my deputy. There was a desk officer for electronic reconnaissance, as well as two officers in the analysis department. There was a general desk officer, who was a warrant officer, and my driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So how many people in total, in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is it five or six? I don't know. A few. So myself, Jovica, Slobo, Jankovic, Mirkovic, six people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Jankovic's name.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you who is this person with the last name of Jankovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a Lieutenant-Colonel at the time. He was in the analysis department. At the time of the events in Srebrenica, he was seconded to the Drina Corps as a communications -- or liaison officer with SFOR or UNPROFOR or whatever it was at the time. It was probably pursuant to a request of the Drina Corps and then his own commander approved it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In military parlance, what does it mean to be seconded?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that on arrival to the unit, he's fully subordinated to the unit commander and receives tasks from him, for a specific period.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when Lieutenant-Colonel Jankovic, because that was his rank at the time, was seconded to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the document itself, and it wasn't important to me. When I arrived there, they told me he had been seconded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who specifically issued tasks to him as the UNPROFOR liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander or the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. I don't know how they regulated it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we look together at 65 ter document 04102? I want to ask you the following. The date of the document is 13 July 1995; in the lower right-hand side corner it is stated that it was sent on 14 July 1995, half an hour after midnight. In the signature block there is the name of Colonel Radoslav Jankovic. Let me ask you this: It was addressed to the Main Staff of the VRS, the OBP sector, and to the command of the Drina Corps, the intelligence department or OB affairs department. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see it, command of the Drina Corps, intelligence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Looking at the document, can you arrive at a conclusion in terms of whether he acted within his mandate as someone who had been seconded to the Drina Corps? That is to say, to inform both the intelligence department of the Main Staff and of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see no problem there. As a responsible officer, he simply included the formation he had come from in this report so that they would be privy to what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When we see -- if we see in the document that it is addressed to the intelligence department -- sector of the Main Staff, who would then be in receipt of this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In one of the paragraphs, I think it is the last one, if we disregard the post scriptum, he says: "The MUP is stealing on a massive scale from UNPROFOR. Today they openly stole their Puch. They wanted to participate in a search of their base after the departure of refugees, which is something I categorically refused." I'm interested in the following. Having regard to Colonel Jankovic's position, did he have any command authority?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at the base. These are issues of morale and ethics. He simply prevented someone from appropriating another's property, and he forwarded that information to the sector and the Drina Corps command. Probably so that from that level, the MUP could be informed in order to put a stop to it. I would have done the same if I had been in his shoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the post scriptum paragraph we see the following: "I think that if we want to take over the enclaves of Zepa and Gorazde in the same way, it will be necessary to present the operation in Srebrenica in the media so as to show that we had rendered adequate treatment to the civilians and even to the soldiers who surrendered their weapons." Let me ask you this: In practical terms, when using such language, who was he proposing to this need to present the operation in Srebrenica in the media? Was it the Main Staff or the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I think that my colleague is asking for speculation because the document speaks for itself, it doesn't mention the word "proposal," and so I don't know where the basis for that question is. And I'm not sure what the basis of the Colonel's information is as to the response that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question has been answered. If it -- in the entirety of the evidence we'll see whether that answer assists us. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, were you ever in a position to see this document in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of 1995, at the time that the operation was being implemented, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, may I put this question to you? You were asked who would have received this letter and you said General Tolimir. Is it right that you were the chief of the intelligence department in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see it is directed to the general's -- the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska intelligence sector. Why didn't you receive it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. The intelligence and security sector. Tolimir was the chief of sector and I was the chief of the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I understand that, but I don't see the term "intelligence and security sector." I only see the term "intelligence sector." I know that there is a difference between sector and administration, but can you explain it? Why is it addressed to the intelligence sector?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, if I may intervene, this is precisely what I wanted to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no, no, sorry, I have put a question to the witness and I would like to hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, what reads here is "sector for OBP," and this stands for "intelligence and security affairs." There was no such thing as an intelligence sector. There was only the intelligence and security sector, and that was its acronym, OBP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a translation problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Salapura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, a translation issue having arisen, I don't know who prepared the translation, whether this is a CLSS translation or not, but it should then perhaps be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we will see to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's precisely what I wanted to say. I thought it was a translation issue. At any rate, thank you for your intervention and assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we look at the translation anyhow, I see that this second addressee or the addressee, that's unclear to me, it says: "To command of the Drina Corps, intelligence department." Now, for the previous one, in bold, I do not see where the bold comes from, as a matter of fact, but there it does not say "to." At the same time it seems that everyone understands the document as having been sent to the general -- the Main Staff of the VRS, and to the command of the Drina Corps. The translation is perhaps a bit confusing in that respect as well, but let's proceed having identified now two possible translation issues. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, on the night between the 12th and the 13th, you were in Bijeljina, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when did you set off for Han Pijesak on the following day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, after breakfast. When exactly, was it 7.00, 8.00, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did two of your associates from the intelligence administration set off with you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Including the driver, yes -- no. They were from the 410th Intelligence Sector. They were programmers in electronics. They were supposed to install a new programme in the administration in order for us to have proper communications with the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where was your first stop on your way to Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Konjevic Polje, at the intersection forking off to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what you were able to see at that point in time, on the 13th of July, in the early morning, at Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Previously, I confused Konjevic Polje and Bratunac -- or, rather, and that pitch. The pitch is not in Konjevic Polje. The pitch is in Kasaba, and I was confusing the two. I only saw vehicles and people moving along over here, nothing special. But I went on my way to Kasaba to the command post of the MP Battalion to ask about the whereabouts of Mladic. I asked where I was -- would be able to find him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you meet with in Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the battalion commander in his office. There was the battalion commander there and the officer operating the switchboard in the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you head to the pitch in Kasaba at any point?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I only exchanged information there, or rather, received information from the commander, and left the place for Bratunac. We were outside within the compound of the battalion command. It was a school, in fact. And he saw me off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall who you got in contact with when you were trying to find out the whereabouts of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The battalion commander. That's Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before he gave you the answer, did he have any sort of telephone communication with anyone to check General Mladic's whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that he did. The soldier operating the switchboard was connecting lines, but there was nothing that was intended for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like us to look at a document but perhaps we should best do it after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break first. The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking in the courtroom. If you want to consult counsel, do it at whisper volume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, over the break I was asked to ask you about the July of 1995. When you were enumerating the individuals working for the intelligence organ in your administration, does the name of Lieutenant-Colonel Petrovic ring any bells? Was he with you in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Petrovic? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: As you were on your way from the school building at Kasaba where you met up with Malinic, did you have to go past the pitch as you were on your way to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had to. The pitch is on the left side of the road, as you head towards Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I have to pause for a moment for interpretation to catch up. In your best estimate, how many prisoners did you believe were present in the pitch?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that in my previous testimonies, that it was very difficult for me to tell. I didn't focus on that. I didn't pay attention to that to be able to give a near estimate. There were many, several hundred people. How many exactly, I don't know. As I arrived there, I saw that some were moving about the pitch, others were lying down. Soldiers were on the edge with their weapons slung over their right shoulder, and it was a rather relaxed atmosphere. But I can't give you any figures. There were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P1256? It's a document under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And I will have questions for you. In fact, this is the reason why I asked you about the number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the previous document, do you want to tender that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I read out the penultimate and last paragraphs so I don't think there is any need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are other parts in that document as well, Mr. Stojanovic, which may be relevant, such as the author of the document saying that he intends to remove a doctor who wants to keep a close eye on whether the sick people are treated well, and that he says, Well, I'll send him away under the pretext that we don't need him any further, which may be relevant as well. Therefore, apart from the translation issue still pending, if you say, I'm not interested in it, the Chamber might be. I leave it in your hands. If you say, I'll not tender it, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I will tell you if we will tender the document or not before the end of my examination. Not at this point because we focused on what was interesting for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you may understand that the Chamber is very interested in what is important for the Defence but not only in what is important for the Defence. Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. First I just want to inform you that we have made a request for the revised translation. And secondly, I wanted to inform the Chamber that to the extent that Mr. Stojanovic may not want to tender the document, I certainly do. So we can resolve it at the end of the witness's evidence, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the document is on the Prosecution exhibit list. In that case, once a revised translation is received, I will tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we reserve a number for that. Madam Registrar? Pending a better translation, the document, and I'm seeking the assistance of my colleagues, 65 ter 418 -- 4102 receives number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall have number P01590, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Yes, it's now tendered by Mr. Stojanovic after some hesitation, so therefore it should receive a D number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. The document 4102 will receive number D306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D306 is marked for identification, and then I take it that the P number which was assigned for only one second is then hereby -- is not valid anymore. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, sir, can you see the document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It is an intercept which reads: "Major Malinic, the commander of the 65th Protective Motorised Regiment Armoured Battalion and Colonel Pero Salapura, the VRS security service, are at the football field in the Kasaba village where they are receiving the arrested Muslims." I have a few things to ask you about concerning the document. First of all, this acronym, commander of OKB in the original, what does it stand for?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can clearly see that it is from the Croatian electronic surveillance service. This is a compilation of different sources, and the summary is quite bad to serve as a report. This is the 13th of July, 1995, at 10.15. When I -- this is when I returned from Bijeljina, and I went directly to the armoured battalion command. I didn't go to any kind of pitch or field, talking to anyone. I asked the commander where General Mladic was and how I could get ahold of him. There was some things that are incorrect here. He's not the commander of the armoured battalion but he commanded the MP Battalion. I wasn't from the security service but from the intelligence service. And I was never at that football pitch. I was on a pitch that is much smaller that was in front of the school, and it was en route to the school. Perhaps it was at around 2.00 or so, and I was asked by one of Malinic's officers to drop by the battalion command since I was with my vehicle, and they said they needed water for their staff. So this is an inexpertly compiled text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I will not have another opportunity to ask about it, someone else who is familiar with this kind of job, and that is why I would want to ask you this. Radio reconnaissance centres, were they in the VRS inside brigades, the corps, or were they directly under the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps did have their radio reconnaissance units, the size of platoon. The Main Staff should have had a radio reconnaissance company but we did not have the necessary equipment and we never developed that kind of unit. The equipment was used mainly to monitor radio and radio relay communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The equipment of the former 5th and 2nd Military District of the JNA, where did it all go to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zagreb. It was left behind because that's where the biggest radio reconnaissance battalion was with the most up-to-date equipment and most of the equipment was left either at the Pleso airport or in the barracks. Only some equipment was pulled out of Zagreb, which was then later on used along certain axes. There were two such devices, I believe, one of which was in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The use of equipment of the former JNA, what happened with it once the JNA withdrew from Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this area, those units were not quite so developed, and most of the equipment was in the war reserves warehouses in Visoko and Kiseljak and that's where it stayed. It was mainly equipment which was rather obsolete or of lower technological quality, and we mostly relied on older equipment and whatever was left in our possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for the time in the document before you, does it tally, to the best of your recollection, with the time when you were in Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came from Bijeljina directly. Perhaps the time was between 10 and 11.00 in the morning. So the time designated on the document may be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to reach Bratunac from Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. It didn't take long but we were stopped along the way. We stayed for some 20 minutes because we were stopped by a soldier who stopped the traffic. On the road, around the bend, there was a group of captured ABiH soldiers, the size of a platoon, so between 20 and 25. I waited in the vehicle and I asked our soldier why the traffic was stopped and whether we could go through. He said that we should wait a little longer and that we couldn't go through because one of the captured fighters tried to activate a hand grenade in order to throw it at the guards who guarded them, so they were waiting for their superior or someone else to clear it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber where could it have all been taking place, as far as you are familiar with the area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kravica, as one enters it, because all of the houses had been burned down, so Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: En route to Bratunac, did you see any larger groups of prisoners anywhere?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see or did you hear some firing on your way to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not on our way to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As you moved along that road, was there other traffic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only a few vehicles that we encountered along the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Who did you meet with in Bratunac when you arrived in the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I dropped by the brigade command and the duty officer was there. I asked him about General Mladic, and where I could find him. He told me he was somewhere in the area of Srebrenica. Since both of the officers who were with me and my driver had not had any breakfast, I asked him to find some food for them. I sat in the vehicle and went to Srebrenica. I planned to come back quickly because I only had some information to share.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a stopover in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never been in that area before. Once I arrived there, I thought it was Srebrenica, but as a matter of fact it was Potocari. That is where I found General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand you quite well. Did you meet General Mladic in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, in Potocari. But at first, I thought it was Srebrenica because I had never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall where you met General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We talked in front of a building, was it a school building or something, but a sizeable building. General Mladic was giving an interview to a TV crew. There were several cameramen. I stood on the side, waiting for it to finish, and I think, as the camera panned out, I was also taped there together with some of the general's escort, his security.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay there talking to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, perhaps up to ten minutes. Yes, when I saw it later, General Mladic took me along. There was a woman there in a house nearby. He went there and he talked to her. That's what I could see later on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we next together look at a short excerpt from the footage which is P1147. This part of the Srebrenica trial video, V 9267. Can we start at 1.37 and end at 2.38.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I wanted you to look at the footage and then I'll have some questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I think we've seen this before, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we did in this part. This is what the reason is, and why I would like you to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then if I am mistaken -- Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I tend to agree with my -- with Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have occasion to see this excerpt before today in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was broadcast on TV, if this is it, and if you continue, I guess you'll see me at the doorstep -- on the doorstep.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise the person behind the woman in this still?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make out the face. I don't know. Perhaps the one on the left is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I'd like to show the last ten seconds, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Janet, please focus on the man in the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's me at the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: Do you now recognise the person behind the woman in this still?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you know, tell us who is the person with the cap, to your right from our angle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is unclear but it's probably one of -- one of Mr. Mladic's security detail. And I don't see he's wearing a cap. Ah-ha.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The person with the cap, who is to the far right in the still?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is completely fuzzy, and I can't remember who it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the name Zvonko Bajagic ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether he was in the same place and at the same time as you that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember whether he was there. I don't remember if Zvonko was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you still believe that this footage was made in Potocari and not in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this excerpt. It is already actually P1147. Apologise. Thank you. If it completely corresponds in terms of the time counter that we relied on. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In that ten-minute conversation that you had with General Mladic, tell us, what was the topic of your discussion and what did General Mladic tell you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the purpose of my coming there. That was why I came from Banja Luka and went to Belgrade. It was the information on the impending attack by the Croatian army on the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. It was the first specific information that we had indicating that these combat activities would most probably spill over to Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, was it necessary, in view of the significance of the information, to convey it to General Mladic in view of the ongoing activities surrounding Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believed that it was. I got there, although I have -- I had some medical problems myself, I thought it was important, and I was there to clear up any of his uncertainties or anything that had to be explained or clarified. There was very little time left before the start of the aggression of the Republic of Serbia against the RSK, and then possibly further activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the information that you conveyed to -- or rather, when you conveyed the information to General Mladic, was there anything that came up concerning Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't discuss Srebrenica at all. I saw that it was being finished. There was quite a lot of old people, women and children. There was this -- what was it, a factory down in Potocari where I saw them. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I inquire with one of the answers? You said there was very little time left before the start of the aggression of the Republic of Serbia against the RSK.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croatia, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is what I thought might be the issue. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At this point, did you receive any sort of instruction from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. General Mladic took notice of it and I did not receive any instructions. I knew that other things needed to be done in that respect, but I wasn't the one who would be taking any measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: This piece of intelligence that you conveyed to General Mladic, did it prove to be true eventually?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The term that I had was the 2nd of August, St. Ilija's day, the attack began two days later, so that was the only thing that proved incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The conversation you had with General Mladic, did it precede or follow the video footage where we saw you, General Mladic and his personal detail?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a dilemma about that but I think that it was after this particular footage. There was first the discussion with journalists and then I spoke to him, and if I recall correctly, then he tapped me on the shoulder and went on to speak to this woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point in time inform General Mladic about what you had seen at Kasaba and on the road from Konjevic Polje to Kravica and Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did. There were quite a few prisoners there already, and probably General Mladic was receiving information from all the units there and was better informed than I was. I was just a person who was passing through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, if I may just get clarity on the witness's answer. Sir, you said: "I had a dilemma about that but I think that it was after this particular footage." Then you say: "There was first the discussion with journalists and then I spoke to him, and if I recall correctly, he tapped me on the shoulder and went to speak with this woman." Now that would mean then that your discussion was before the footage, not after the footage. You are giving -- if he tapped you and then went and spoke to the woman, the footage can only be taken at a time when he speaks with the woman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you spoke to him before the footage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I see whether I can resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to cut matters short. In your previous testimony, you were talking about the footage outside where you were at a distance of 30 metres from General Mladic. Your previous testimony was that you then had a conversation with him after that footage and that this visit followed your conversation. Is that a correct understanding of your testimony given in another case and in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may explain it all now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please, first --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because there is some sort of misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So when I asked you whether this is a correct understanding, your answer is: No, it's not a correct understanding. My next question would be in what respect is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you're not wrong. Perhaps I am. When I arrived, General Mladic was engaged in an interview with journalists and I was some 10 or 15 metres behind him waiting for him to finish the interview. When it finished, I approached him and we greeted each other and I told him that I had certain things to inform him about. And then in some first statements of mine, I seem to have left out this moment with the woman because I focused on what it was that I was telling him, and when I saw this footage now, I recall that he tapped me on the shoulder, he took me up to that house, he spoke to that woman, it didn't last long, and then as we got out of the house, I took him to one side and that was when I shared information with him. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we have footage 1, outdoors; footage 2, indoors, with the lady; and after that a conversation. That is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Salapura, is it possible that you have a problem with your chair?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it's all right. It's a bit steep but it's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I think with the back of your chair --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't dare lean back because I might go all the way down, but it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, then it's not all right. It should be fixed so that you can't fall over at the back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't. I'm leaning against the desk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The usher will assist you but he has to find one of the knobs below the seat rather than -- have you fixed -- it's the left handle if it's the same chair, just left hand, there is a knob which can fix. Is that better?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think Judge Moloto still has a problem with the sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question put to you, sir, was, and this is at page 32, lines 20 to 22: "The conversation you had with General Mladic, did it precede or follow the video footage where we saw you, General Mladic and his personal detail?" Now, your explanation you've just given to Judge Orie now is that you had a discussion with General Mladic, you told him that you wanted to talk to him, he patted you on the shoulder, you went into the house, then the footage was taken, and then after you talked to him about the Krajina. Now, the conversation that I thought Mr. Stojanovic had in mind when he asks you about the conversation is the conversation about the Krajina. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So it took up -- is it now your explanation that it took place after the footage? Not before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- it seems to me that that's the case. If it's so important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank -- it's not very important. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Following your conversation with General Mladic, which of the two of you left the place where it was all happening first? You or General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further gesture to the public audience will result in measures taken by this Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Mr. Mladic wants to consult you. Inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you stop at the Bratunac Brigade on your way back?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did drop by the Bratunac Brigade. I collected the two IT officers and my driver because I was driving myself from Bratunac to Potocari. I left them behind to have their meal and then we all went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your best estimate, at what time did you meet again in the Bratunac Brigade HQ?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At around noon, 1.00 p.m. I'm not sure. I can't say. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to come across anyone from the corps command of the Bratunac Brigade at the brigade's headquarters?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did. I think it was the duty officer who was there only.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the assistant commander for intelligence and security in the Bratunac Brigade, Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't personally know him. I had heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you see him at any point during the day? Did you come across him? Did you exchange any words with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, did you have any sort of communications device in your vehicle?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On your way back from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje and Kasaba, did you spot any larger groups of prisoners at any point along that road?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group that was there previously, on my incoming journey, was no longer there on my way back. I didn't observe anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stop by the pitch at Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On my return, a non-commissioned officer pulled the vehicle over and asked that I drop by the battalion HQ and the commander Malinic because he wanted me to convey information that they had no water. They had no water to spare for the prisoners or even the soldiers there who were guarding them, and he wanted them to be provided with water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And did you convey this -- so did you drop by and see Malinic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do anything to find ways and means to supply the prisoners and soldiers with water?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I conveyed that information to Malinic, and I suppose that he, as a commander, saw to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Outside the HQ of the -- Malinic's unit, did you see any UNPROFOR vehicles?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at the time, I don't think so. There were just a couple of his soldiers outside. I don't recall seeing an UNPROFOR vehicle. I saw UNPROFOR vehicles in Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask for one clarification. Mr. Salapura, you told us that Mr. Malinic wanted you to convey information that they had no water for the prisoners and for his soldiers. Then some lines down, you said, this is line 11 on page 38, "I conveyed that information to Malinic." Which information did you convey to Malinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, either there was a difficulty in interpretation or misunderstanding. On my way back from Bratunac, there was a non-commissioned officer of his, right? Who was there standing by the venue where the prisoners were, by the pitch. He waved to me to stop over and asked me to drop by the battalion's HQ and to see the battalion commander and tell them that we had no water -- they had no water.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ah, now I understand. It was the non-commissioned officer who wanted you to convey the message that they don't have water to Mr. Malinic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Malinic was to make sure that they were supplied with water.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel, for this clarification. My next question is this: Did you, at any time during your stay in Kasaba, have occasion to meet Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see Beara as of the moment I went on sick leave, and later on, even during the time when I was there, he wasn't at the command post. I didn't see him anymore. I only saw him sometime in August, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, after having stopped in Kasaba, did you -- did you spend any time anywhere before your arrival in Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were stopped by the police on the road from Kasaba -- well, perhaps one or two kilometres away, at a bend. They told us that there was no further passage possible towards Vlasenica because they had a problem with members of the 28th Division because there was an exchange of fire. One could hear bursts of fire shortly afterwards. Then things became quiet. I stayed there for some time. Later, they told me -- well, I asked to be let through to go to the command post because things were quiet, but they said they couldn't let me pass just yet, and I told them I would go at my own responsibility because my plan was to go to Banja Luka the same day. They approved my passage. I armoured the vehicle and went.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay in Vlasenica in the Drina Corps command?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go there, to the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when did you arrive in the Main Staff facility at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in the afternoon. I can't be more specific than that. I can't recall the hour. I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, who did you find, then, at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the hut where I worked, going to the office where my analysts were. I brought the other two along and they unloaded their stuff. Only Slobodan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat the last name.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was there and Bora, the warrant officer who was the desk officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us the family name of Slobodan again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mamlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber whether you saw any of the Main Staff officers at the VRS Main Staff command.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I encountered anyone passing through. It was my intention to go back immediately. I had some back problems, so I took some time to rest, but it didn't work out, so I dropped the idea of returning and postponed it until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When did you, in fact, leave the Main Staff facility at Crna Rijeka? When did you leave the area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left the facility on the 18th because the next day, as of early morning, the road was closed for all traffic, from Vlasenica further afield, until further notice, which was the 18th, as it turned out. Starting with the 14th in the morning. Or maybe even the 13th in the evening. Yes. At the briefing, at Miletic's, Mamlic told him the road was blocked for traffic from Vlasenica onwards and that it should be conveyed to all of the officers at the Main Staff that they could not use the road from Vlasenica to Zvornik until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that time, as of the 13th, late in the afternoon, until the 18th when you left Crna Rijeka, did you at any point find yourself in a situation to meet with General Mladic and talk to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that General Mladic, at the time, was away on business for a while to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The facility where you were physically present in those few days, is it physically separated from the building where General Mladic would be if he were to be at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The buildings are separate. When he dropped by, he usually went to the building where the Chief of Staff and the operations head was. It was in that hut.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, at some point in time, assist Tribunal investigators to identify the buildings and the offices in terms of who was sitting where in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of those four days or less than four days, while you were at the Main Staff, did you have occasion to meet Beara at any time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I told you already I didn't see Beara until August.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During the four days, did you happen to run into General Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see General Tolimir and I didn't even speak to him on the phone because he was in the area of Rogatica and Zepa. He was in charge of that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because I would like us to go through a number of intercepts together. Before that, could you tell the Chamber when did you meet General Mladic? How far back does your acquaintance with him go?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he took over his duty as the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: While you were still with the JNA, until the war broke out in Croatia, did you have an opportunity to meet General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war broke out in 1992 in Bosnia, you were with the 2nd Military District Command in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the 5th in Zagreb and then it was renamed to become the 2nd and stationed in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you leave Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As part of the column in Dobrovoljacka Street. We were attacked. There were many casualties before we managed to pull out or get through.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you also wounded? Were you hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't wounded, although I still have back problems. I've had those problems for some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, I'm looking at the clock, that's one. I think it's time for a break. Could the witness follow the usher. We will take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will take a break and resume at ten minutes past mid-day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Could I inquire with you, Mr. Stojanovic, whether you're on track in terms of time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think I will definitely conclude my cross-examination today, as was planned, or perhaps earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, we stopped at the moment when we were discussing your previous contact with General Mladic. Please tell the Chamber whether you had an opportunity to follow Mr. Mladic during negotiation with the enemy side at any point during the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked a lot with UNPROFOR representatives and representatives of the international community, so my answer is yes, and it was through mediation of one or another international representative.
