That was in Sarajevo at the airport. But General Tolimir was more in charge of that, or he followed him around more. Outside the few times, I don't remember having encountered him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the performance of your duties, did you have contact during the war with the Croatian side, as a participant to the war events?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Both the Croatian and the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a situation to convey any requests by Croats for assistance to be provided to civilians?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did convey such requests to General Mladic, coming from both the Croatian and Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you cite an example when you were asked by an enemy side to provide assistance on the part of the RS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I was in charge of such talks, as well as my counterparts on the other side. Zepce, the Croatian side, we accepted to provide full support and supply because they had been completely encircled. We even received their wounded and sick to be treated in Banja Luka, in the hospital. I think that was in 1994 or 1995. There is more, sorry. Let's talk about the Muslim side. For example, East and West Mostar was divided and the population on the east side was in a difficult situation. I was engaged in talks surrounding the issue, and I received approval from General Mladic to provide supplies to the eastern part, to the Muslim population, through our territory. We also did not make use of a very unfavourable tactical situation that the Muslims found themselves in due to their conflict with the Croatian side and we did not get engaged in the conflict because if we had, we would probably have gained some territory but there would have been numerous casualties among both civilians and the military. The same would have probably happened with Zepce.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In such contacts you had concerning these requests by the Croatian and Muslim military and civilian authorities, which you conveyed to General Mladic, what was his position in that regard?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A positive one, and ultimately it was done according to his decision. There was another example, when the Muslim-Croat conflict erupted in late 1993, the Croats in the Lasva Valley and around Vlasic were in a very difficult situation. They had nowhere to go. And in the evening, I remember, I personally approached General Mladic at his resting place and explained the situation. I suggested that we should receive both the civilians and HVO soldiers in Herceg-Bosna to let them pass through our territory and then to let them go where they wanted to go. We even received their soldiers with their weapons. In my view, it was one of the most humane actions in the whole war in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a situation to accompany Mr. Mladic during the war, when he went to Russia?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What kind of international contact was there between the Russian authorities and the military authorities of the RS and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were direct contacts, but verbal contacts, without much practical substance, in terms of any significant aid or anything of the sort. They went up to the level of minister, the Minister of Defence and the Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As the intelligence officer, did you have any contact during the war with the French government and the French military authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with the government, but I did have contact with the French military envoy, and we were in frequent contact. It was quite normal. They always sought contact, not only through the diplomatic corps but with military envoys, and it concerned a number of countries throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether, in that period, as of June 1995 until September 1995, were there any French intelligence elements in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. The French contingent was in Sarajevo as part of UNPROFOR. They probably did have their security and intelligence personnel as part of the contingent. All of the countries that were members of UNPROFOR and SFOR did so, and that's quite standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As an officer of the intelligence administration of the VRS Main Staff, did you have any counter intelligence or other tasks which had to do with the work of intelligence services of the countries comprising UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My service did not engage in counter-intelligence work. It was done by the security service. I don't know. I did not receive such information from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In all such contacts you had with General Mladic concerning the provision of assistance to the Croatian and Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you at any point in time come across a lack of understanding or a position expressed by General Mladic not to assist them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think he talked directly to the municipal president in East Mostar at that time. It was Safet Orucevic [Realtime transcript read in error "Irucevic"], I believe, or as far as I recall. So General Mladic was in personal contact with him. It is not Irucevic but Orucevic, in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 47, line 13 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, let me go back to the time when you spent those four days at the Main Staff. What were your specific duties on the four days between the 14th and the 17th of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I visited the doctor on two occasions, and I didn't have any duties. You can see that best in the transcript from the Tolimir case, when I was a Prosecution witness in that case. As I left for my sick leave, the agreement was that in the eastern part he should be in charge of intelligence, and during my stay in Banja Luka, while on sick leave, I was to coordinate the work between the intelligence organs of the 1st and 2nd Corps and the 410th Intelligence Centre. Those four days that I was there, I was waiting for the road to become passable so that I may leave. I did not take part in planning or decision making. I wasn't charged with any assignments or duties. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I asked you this because I want us to look at some intercepts together which we would ask you to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at P1362? And we should mind the fact that the document is under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I will not read out the heading because the document is under seal, but if you can see, it says 17 July 1995, and then we look at the first two registered contacts. Please pay attention to 1115 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, where the B/C/S version is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, Your Honours, we'll go through this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Apparently X and Y are speaking together?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: X says -- or, rather, Y says: "It's me calling you again." X says: "The line is not very -- I can't hear you very well, you know." Y says: "I don't know what's wrong." "X: Speak up. "Y: Set off this way. "X: Say it again? "Y: Has Keserovic set off? "X: Well, we met him when we were on our way here. "Y: Well, he hasn't come to me yet. "X: Well, in that case he might have first gone ahead over there to Momir Nikolic's. "Y: Uh-huh. So, you know, I spoke a little earlier with General Miletic." I'll stop here for a moment and ask you this: Do you know who Keserovic is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of July, do you know what duty he was discharging and where he was?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was the desk officer for the military police within the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity over those four days to meet Keserovic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll continue reading the text. Y says: "He told me that Keserovic is also supposed to come over here to deal with these issues." X says: "Right. "Y: But what I told you this morning -- X says: "I told the commander, he ordered Salapura and an order will be written or, rather, a request to the MUP for all of them to return. Or rather be kept there." "Y: Well, here there are going, the buses are there, they are assembling, they've got your order." X says: "Well, I know. Well, Salapura spoke with Kovacevic and got a verbal approval that a shift would be coming during the day. "Y: I know. But you can see the people here are already setting off." Let me stop here for a moment. Does this conversation make you recall any assignments you might have had on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th? The commander didn't give me any orders on the 17th, and I didn't have anything to do with any sort of transport or anything else. Throughout my time up there I was at the command post, in the hut and in my office. On the 16th, I was at the doctor's, and on the 17th I was given sick leave by my doctor again for some 20 days or a month, and I wasn't getting involved at all. I don't know who this Kovacevic is. I didn't speak to any Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't know where this Kovacevic would be, who that person would be, by that last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I wanted to look at this, to have this clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look up P1361 in e-court? Again, the document is under seal. Can we have -- yes, page 1 of the English version, as we have it. At one point, as I'm reading, I'll ask that we turn to the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'll quickly go through the transcript. It's handwritten this time. As I was reading just now, the text is identical up to the point that I will now read out. X says -- or, rather, Y says: "However, what I told you this morning --" X responds: "I told the commander he ordered Salapura and the order will be drafted or, rather, a request to the MUP to bring all of them back. Or rather to keep them. Y - and can we now turn to the next page in the B/C/S - "Well, they are leaving, the buses are collecting or are assembling, they have your order." Now, look at this handwritten version. It reads: "I know, Salapura talked to Kovac and got his -- and got a verbal approval or consent that the shift will arrive in the course of the day." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anyone by the last name of Kovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that in this part, the intercept was substantially changed from Kovacevic to Kovac?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I had no contact whatsoever with Kovac. I didn't know where he was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of this text, would you be able to tell us who X or Y are?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what this is about, what buses, what, and no order, it was only Commander Mladic who could have issued me with an order but I didn't receive any on the 17th, 16th, 15th, 14th or the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. And can I ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, just for my understanding, you said the intercept was changed from Kovacevic and Kovac. Now, do we know in which order they were created? We apparently have two versions. I'm a bit lost about the one version and the other version because I think I remember that I saw some handwriting in the previous one as well. I don't know whether the parties can -- the witness apparently has got no idea about what it's all about so it doesn't make that much sense to ask him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear, Mr. Salapura. I now see that we have a -- the previous one we saw was written, typewritten, and do I have to understand that there was a handwritten version and that it then was transformed in a typewritten version, and that they are more or less separately translated and that's why we have two versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In substance, Mr. President, that's about it. There is a witness that's coming that I think can shed some light on the practice and procedures concerning these intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at this moment, so when you said, Mr. -- let me check that exactly. One second, please. Yes. One second again. Yes. When you said that the intercept was changed from Kovacevic to Kovac, if I understood you well, but I'll verify that immediately, that the logical order is that it went the other way around. That is, the handwritten version, which I take it was the first one, because you usually do not produce a handwritten version if there is already a typewritten version, in the handwritten version, it says "Kovac" and in the typewritten version it says "Kovacevic." So it was not changed from Kovacevic to Kovac but just the other way around. Yes. But that's not what you -- well, it's not -- it's perhaps not without relevance, Mr. Stojanovic, but apparently I do understand that we agree that that was a -- perhaps not a confirmed and logically accurate line. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's precisely right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has not got to do with anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We will see how it unfolds, but I do believe in the chronology of events the handwritten version came first. Colonel, my question was: In view of the difference in the transcripts, you stand by what you said, that you were not engaged in any sort of conversation with either an individual by the last name of Kovacevic or an individual by the last name of Kovac on that day?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do stand by that, absolutely. And I can also state the same for the people from the intelligence organ, that none of them were engaged in these issues about transporting people, buses, et cetera, except for the battalion where there is one person dealing with the intelligence and the brigade as well. And there was only a handful of us and we could not afford ourselves the luxury to deal with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, when I asked you about the name of Kovac, you said yes, of course, you knew him, that it was the Minister of the Interior. But would it refresh your memory if I were to tell you that at the time he was Deputy Minister of the Interior and that an individual by the name of Zivko Rakic was, to all intents and purposes, the Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that he was a Minister of the Interior but was it at that time, I didn't have any special cooperation with the Ministry of the Interior save for a rare contact. I did have cooperation with the State Security Service but not with the Ministry of the Interior, only rarely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one thing. Thinking about the structures and the events, was there a role for Mr. -- for the Ministry of the Interior to be played in that context as we read that in this intercept? Apart from whether you had contacts or not, but was there any role for the Ministry of the Interior in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here? I don't see specifically what it was that MUP was doing here, a shift was supposed to come and some people were supposed to be transported somewhere. I really don't know what the role of the MUP would have been. As I told you, I wasn't involved in it at all and I don't even know who participated in these operations, which specific units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was not talking about the units. I was talking about the role to be played by the minister or the deputy minister --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Deputy minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but the higher-up authorities in the Ministry of the Interior. Was there a -- could you imagine of any role in the context of what we see here to be played by them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what this is about at all. From what I can see, I don't know what this is about. I can't grasp the point of it. Was it a combat activity, transportation of troops, transportation of prisoners, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it was about combat activity, was there a role to be played by the Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know to what extent and how the Ministry of the Interior participated in this operation, the units, or in which capacity, I’m not aware of it. Was it as they were resubordinated to the army or separately? You have to understand that I did not participate in the operation and I don't know who did. I happened to be there by accident and I did not interfere with the processes that were unfolding. I was there waiting every single day to be able to return. I was not privy to this information. I did not receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If MUP units were engaged there, would their deployment and possible resubordination to the army, would that need the approval of the Minister of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think so. I saw the MUP units, as I said in the statement. They stopped me on the road. Those MUP units were engaged in an exchange of fire with members of the 28th Division that were trying to pull out towards Tuzla, from two sides, and the road was passing right in between them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, in your last answer, you said talking about the MUP, "I'm not aware of them participating in any capacity." And then in the next answer you describe how you saw them there involved in activities. Any explanation for this -- what could be considered as a discrepancy between your previous answer and the last answer? You said, "Those MUP units were engaged in an exchange of fire with members of the 28th Division ..." That comes as a surprise if we have learned from you that you were not aware of them participating in any capacity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said, that I didn't know in what capacity they were there, but as I was explaining my arrival, I told you there were MUP members there who stopped me on the road from Kasaba to Han Pijesak. They stopped me and said there was an exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not what you said. That was not what your testimony is, unless you challenge the accuracy of the translation and the transcription. If so, do not hesitate to do it. We'll verify it on the basis of the audio and then we will establish whether or not you said: "Those MUP units were engaged in an exchange of fire with members of the 28th Division that they were -- they were trying to pull out towards Tuzla and the road was passing right in between them." If you say, "That's not what I said," then we'll verify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Perhaps not in so many words but I said that I was stopped by the MUP members on the road, that there was an exchange of fire, and that I asked them to let me through on my own responsibility, and that they did. I didn't explain anything further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are evading the point I'm making, that at one moment you say, "I wasn't even aware that they were engaged at all," and in your next answer you tell us and you explain to us what they were doing there at the time. That could be considered to be contradictory or inconsistent. I'm asking for an explanation and you have until now not given that explanation. Therefore, we will proceed. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we replay the -- this part to see what I said, so that I can listen to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We cannot replay it but it will be verified. I asked you earlier whether you challenged it. You said no. Now I do understand that you do challenge it. This portion will be reviewed. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, which road did you take on the 18th to leave Crna Rijeka and go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through Vlasenica. So I went from Vlasenica to Zvornik and then Bijeljina. On the 18th, the road was open for traffic. And on the 18th, my assistant Karanovic arrived from Belgrade, and he was also supposed to arrive on the 13th or the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were asked about the route. You have given that answer. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic, and once an answer is given, please put your next question to the witness. Mr. Mladic, audio problems? If there are any audio problems -- no, Mr. Mladic, no loud speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that the last answer did not make it into the transcript, I wanted to ask you -- actually that Mr. Mladic didn't hear it, I wanted to ask you whether you saw any police elements along that road.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I was definitely not stopped anywhere. And I don't think I saw anyone along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Trying to conclude on the topic of chronology, I'd like to ask you just this question. As of the 18th of July, 1995, how long did you stay in the Krajina, i.e., when did you return to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed there until -- I think until September or until the Dayton Accords or just before. When was the Dayton? Yes, I was there almost up to the Dayton Accords themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall when you met General Mladic again?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in August, at Ostrelj. He wanted me there. I was still on sick leave. I arrived at Ostrelj by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the topic of your discussion and why did he want to see you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was also concerning the attack of the Croatian army on the Krajina. That was the topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, was there any discussion concerning the Srebrenica and Zepa events?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We only focused on the situation unfolding in the area. The attack on the Krajina had already begun and the units were pulling out from Krajina via Ostrelj and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness mention the last location, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last location you mentioned? You said pulling out from Krajina via Ostrelj and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between Bosanski Petrovac and Drvar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, do you hail from that area?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was your family forced to move due to the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was abroad and returned, but that was later, when the attack was prolonged or actually when it carried over into Republika Srpska. My mother was left alone, and the neighbours managed to bring her to the area of Banja Luka. I arrived a bit late for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Allow me to put a few questions about the intercepts. Given that I suppose you're familiar with the methodology of that kind of work, tell us, please, by your experience in terms of intelligence work and reconnoitring radio communication by the enemy side, such omissions as we saw a moment ago concerning the first and last name, is that possible?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It frequently happens, even nowadays. For example, the MUP. There is a frequent mix-up between the security and intelligence service. Even now, when I'm introduced by someone from the MUP, they say, This is the man from the security service. And I say, I'm from the intelligence. And they say, Well, to us it's the same. But it's not. It's possible that someone had another service in mind and another person and my name came up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We need to pause between questions and answers in order to avoid overlaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please wait until the question is entirely put and not yet start answering before Mr. Stojanovic, his words, have been pronounced and have been translated by the interpreters and written down by the transcribers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some problems with the functioning of e-court, although LiveNote is still working. I suggest that we proceed up until the moment where we are so much bothered by the technical problems that we will take a break. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'll follow from my colleague's monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, this last answer, when I asked you about the reliability and possible mistakes when intercepting radio relay communication, could you briefly repeat your answer because not all of it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said it is possible, and that the mixing up of positions is possible, especially when it comes to, for example, this Kovac. If one were to ask him today where I come from, he would say the security service.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, given your experience and work in the process of intercepting radio relay communications, omissions or mistakes such as the one with the last name, are they possible and how do they happen?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are mistakes that are possible. However, there should be the original documents pertaining to the conversations recorded. So a mistake can be made by the person recording it or by the person in the reconnaissance unit and, lastly, it can also happen with the person processing the text. So much depends on that and who used that information ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, could the warring parties be aware of such radio relay communication being followed by the enemy side?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew it throughout, we knew we were being monitored. We monitored their communications and they did ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In military parlance, operational masking or jamming, what does it mean? And did the VRS use it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It includes a spectrum of measures and activities, resulting in disseminating misinformation. It includes a number of tactical measures and activities, fake manoeuvres, and transmitting fake information on the air. Even misinformation in terms of the axis of attack can be intentionally wrong and then it turns out an attack occurred on a different axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reliability of intercepts based on your experience in 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was assessed. Our analysts always designated the degree of reliability. And we, intelligence men, when we received information we also designated it with the degree of reliability. Sometimes we would say it is correct or that it needs to be checked or probably correct. Or that it needs to be verified and only taken note of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To conclude, let us touch upon the topic of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. During examination-in-chief, at some point, you mentioned an activity that the 10th Sabotage Detachment had with regards to Srebrenica. What did you have in mind? Kindly tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean before this operation was carried out or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. June 1995.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Isn't it the 13th? There was a sabotage operation which was planned and executed on Srebrenica. It was supposed to be cautionary in nature, to send a message to the command and leadership in Srebrenica to cease sabotage and incursions into RS territory. When this operation took place in parallel with our preparations, they were preparing another operation aimed at our territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get that information from, which then you used as the basis to plan a sabotage operation by the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the service was aware of the situation in Srebrenica up to 90 per cent. There were several sources of information, and one of such sources was electronic surveillance although not to a large extent, but we also had direct information. The service did have their own man there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say it had its own man, who did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A specific person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "there" --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on the information you got, were you able to make a realistic assessment of the condition of the units present in the Srebrenica enclave?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could I ask one question to seek clarification. You said there was a sabotage operation which was planned and executed on Srebrenica. Were you -- you were involved in the preparation of that action or in the planning of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is there any -- are there any plans, is there any paperwork, which develops orders given that this was to be meant a separate operation apparently from taking over the enclave, or is -- or did I misunderstand you? You said it was intended to be of a cautionary nature. Now, I understand that there is a difference between the taking over of an enclave and to have a sabotage operation with a cautionary nature. Do you -- could you provide us with further information as to how that sabotage operation was prepared, had it a code name, who was giving instructions to whom, and where we can clearly see that it was not part of the taking over of the enclave, because that's, as I understand, is your view on what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. The operation was carried out, as far as I remember, at the request of the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps, or the command of the Drina Corps, General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was more whether there was any paperwork which clearly shows that this is apart from the whole of the operation of taking over the enclave of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, absolutely. They were drafted at the level of the detachment. There are instructions and I do believe that the Tribunal, the Prosecution, have specific documents where this can be seen. For instance, I can tell you, upon full responsibility, that I wasn't aware of the fact that the operation for the takeover of Srebrenica was being planned. I wasn't aware of it at all and, of course, didn't participate in it. I was surprised to receive information that Srebrenica had been taken, and I was in Banja Luka at the time, I was on sick leave, and I didn't know that the operation was being planned. And this operation was absolutely carried out independently of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was at what point in time, you said? I'm just trying to -- was that on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, June, June. Or actually, sorry, 23 June. That was my mistake. I confused it with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there was some -- the transcript was not -- yes, June is mentioned. Then it says, "Isn't it the 13th?" Yes, now it's clear to me. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic. Or should we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's an error, yes, not the 13th but the 23rd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stojanovic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for making that mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps this is the right time for our break and I will then finish in the next ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the next ten minutes. Another option would be to continue for another ten minutes, but I'm looking at you and Mr. Mladic as well, and then to have a -- perhaps we take the break now. We will take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00. First the witness will be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, kindly take -- tell the Chamber, to the best of your recollection, when did you receive information about what had been happening with some members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment in July 1995 from the commander of that detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the operatives of the 410th Intelligence Centre who informed me about it, on the premises of the centre. They told me the stories that probably originated from the members of the detachment -- these members of the detachment. I asked them where the commander was. He was on annual leave at the time, but he was in Bijeljina, so I called him and told him to come to the premises of the sub-centre of the 410th Intelligence Centre -- the sub-centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was when you received information. So let's start with the when and then Mr. Stojanovic may have other questions for you. When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't set a precise date. Was it late December or early January, it's hard for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In those days of July 1995, was the unit militarily engaged or was it resting?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I didn't give the unit its missions, and I didn't participate in its preparations. However, what I heard was that the unit was engaged in the combat activities which were supposed to make way into Srebrenica. Apparently General Krstic asked that the unit be engaged for this assignment. It was resubordinated to the command of the Drina Corps for those purposes. It entered the town itself and completed its mission without any losses.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Once it had completed its mission, did you have any information to the effect that one of the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment was killed in a traffic accident?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told yes, that the APC skidded off and rolled over, and that was when I came to the command post, when I asked about the detachment. I called the command post of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and then the duty officer told me that the unit had participated in the operations in Srebrenica, that it was given 10 days of leave, that the soldiers were currently on furlough. My next question was where the commander was. And he told me that the commander was injured and that he was on sick leave. I asked him was it serious? He said no. And that was it. That was the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Following all these months and the discussion with the commander, did he tell you how it came to that, that the soldiers would be engaged?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did say since they were resting, how come these soldiers were there and he told me that these were soldiers who simply had nowhere to go because their home was further away. They were soldiers from the territory of the Federation or who had fled that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you at any point that he was involved in any way in the fact that these soldiers went to Pilica and Branjevo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, Please just answer the questions that I put to you. Did you order that or did you participate in the issuing of orders for the engagement in such operations? He said not. Then I asked him, Did you have anything to do with it? He said no. Then I said, Very well. And from what I remember, my words, I told him I'm not interested in anything else. This is a problem and those whose shoe pinches in this matter should deal with it. And that was my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you at any point inform General Mladic of the extent of your conversation with the commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform General Tolimir of the content of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you at any point in such a situation that, following the signing of the Dayton Accords, you would speak to General Mladic about the specific members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, tell us, could the members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment have been engaged by anyone from the security organs at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but I don't think so, because under the rules, and I can speak about the rules, this is part of the preparations for combat, where you see which units will be in charge of providing security to the area, who will be in charge of gathering prisoners, which -- who will be equipping which camps, who will be in charge of transportation, escort, security, et cetera, but as I said, I wasn't involved in the planning so I can't tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You said at one point, and I will finish on this score, that the 10th Sabotage Detachment was involved in the Srebrenica operations and was resubordinated to the Drina Corps at the request of General Krstic. I'm asking you this as a professional soldier: If one of these soldiers committed a crime, any criminal offence, who within the system of the Army of Republika Srpska would be supposed to take steps to prosecute such individuals?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firstly, the unit commander would have to inform the security organs who, in turn, would have to gather information and get in touch with the prosecutor. Next, at the request of the prosecutor, they would have to gather enough evidence to enable the prosecutor to initiate criminal proceedings before a military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a clarification. Would the military police not be involved in that exercise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Probably the military police would be involved at a certain point because it's subordinated to the security organs and to the commander. Depending on what their assessment would be, probably the forensic officers of the military police would be engaged as well. We did not have any inspectors in the military police. We only had scene-of-crime examiners, forensic officers who could secure the area, fix the traces, et cetera. And the security officers would be dealing with the elements preceding the charges that would be brought by the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One short and simple question, please a short and simple answer as well: Was the military police to investigate any crimes committed by members of the army? Or was it the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a task for the security service. It should have organised it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The military police receives from their superior, the chief of security, what their tasks are in that regard. As opposed to the civilian police, the MUP, I have to stress yet again that the military police did not have people in charge of investigations. They could only document crimes for the sake of security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then if, as the question was put by Mr. Stojanovic, if one of the soldiers has committed a crime, who would arrest that soldier, if not the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the military police, they would arrest the people. It arrests, brings in, detains and guards the prisons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question because you just said to us: "As opposed to the civilian police, the MUP, I have to stress yet again, that the military police did not have people in charge of investigations." Surely they don't just arrest. They must arrest and investigate, don't they? To be able to give a docket to the prosecutor, the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They did not have inspectors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not talking about inspectors.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and people for investigations. Military police units were military units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, let's just stop there. I'm not talking about inspectors. I'm talking about investigating. Once they are arrested, they are arrested because of some suspicion, they must investigate that to see whether, in fact, they have a case to put before the prosecutor. Shouldn't they do that? Isn't that part of their remit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. Scene-of-crime officers can do that to the extent possible, to take pictures, evidence, objects used to commit the crime, the location of the crime, et cetera. That's within their remit. As for security officers, they arrange any further procedure with the prosecutor, and they coordinate the work. The prosecutor's office takes over the entire case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will conclude, Colonel, with the following question: When you say the security organs of a unit, in the situation of resubordination, who -- which is the unit whose security organs would be in charge of the Main Staff, the corps or the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In cases of subordination, when the task was -- is being implemented, then it is the security organs of the Drina Corps. Now, believe me, I don't know who of the security officers was in charge for the 10th Sabotage Detachment, in terms of security. In other words, to deal with the information regarding the unit. Perhaps they had an associate, someone who worked for them in the detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel. We have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Vanderpuye, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. President, I don't think I'll be able to finish in the 15 or 20 minutes we have left. I just wanted to advise the Chamber of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course which triggers immediately the next question. How much time do you think you'll need if more than 15 or 20 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think closer to half an hour to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, let me just start where my colleague Mr. Stojanovic left off. And that is on the question of responsibility, once there is knowledge of a crime that's been committed by a soldier. As a professional soldier, are you aware of your obligation when you come into knowledge of a fact that a crime has been committed, particularly a serious one such as the ones you were alerted to, what your responsibility is to report that crime?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I learned about it, I believe everyone else must have known about it by that time. Those who were supposed to know must have known far in advance of myself. For the most part, I was absent. I only appeared in the area, when was it, but there were officers there working on it, and the MUP, the police, so it's not about one person. It's everyone. Everyone knew probably. What was done, how much. It is the security service that was in charge of it. Whether they worked on gathering information, perhaps covertly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm stopping you there. The question was what your responsibility was. Now you have told us about the responsibilities of almost everyone else. The question was about your responsibility. If this is all to say that there was no responsibility for you, then just say none. But don't start explaining that it was everyone's responsibility because everyone knew and earlier and -- what was your responsibility when you learned about it? Could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer it. In terms of my position, I did not have any obligation to either investigate or deal with it. But as an officer, yes, perhaps I could have -- go to the security service and talked to a colleague from the security service about where things were at that moment, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, I'm again have to stop you. You said: "In terms of my position, I did not have any obligation to either investigate or deal with the matter." That's it. Then to say but as an officer, your position was that of an officer, so you are not invited to give two different answers to the same question. You said you had no obligation to either investigate or deal with it. Next question, please, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As a senior, high-ranking officer of the Main Staff, above the corps level, are you saying that as an officer in that position, you had no obligation whatsoever to report the crimes, particularly the very serious crimes that you indicated in your previous evidence in the Tolimir case were horrifying and that you couldn't wrap your head around the scale of those crimes? Did you think as a senior-ranking officer in the Main Staff of the VRS, that you had no obligation to report that, or did you not report that because you were aware that everyone else knew about it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Absolutely what? There are two options given.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you not report this crime because you knew that other members of the Main Staff were fully aware of it, both how horrifying it was, and of its scale and who committed it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or was it -- that is the other part of the question, or was it that you had no obligation to report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It is correct. I heard there, and also from my operatives that I talked to, and everyone already knew that. I think it had already leaked into the town, let alone the army. So I thought it was a process that was underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me then try to see whether I correctly understood your answer. Do you intend to say that there was an obligation to report but that there was no need to do that any further because everyone knew already? Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I believed everyone knew, and from what I learned when I talked to my operatives, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Mr. Vanderpuye will put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to see if I can get some clarification, Colonel. When you say "everyone knew," you mean everyone in the Main Staff knew, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in mind the competent organs from the security service, starting from the battalion up, and probably at the Main Staff, at least the people who worked in that area or on that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just come right to it, then. You knew at the time that you received this information that everyone in the Main Staff knew, including General Mladic, about those crimes, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that everybody knew. I can't say that. Most did. For example, some of my desk officers may have well been unaware. They were busy with their own thing and did not have much contact with others, but realistically speaking, yes, probably many people knew because it was a sizeable operation. Those people needed to be transported, logistics units engaged, transport organised, engineering -- the engineering corps activated, so many people were probably engaged in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I take you back to one of your previous answers? You said: "Everyone knew, I think even the whole town knew about it, let alone the army," which is language which suggests that at least everyone in the army knew and that many outside the army knew as well. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Absolutely, absolutely. Certainly people outside the army knew. I can't say everyone in the army knew, but many locals knew, people who saw things in the area as well as people from the MUP, the members of the MUP, the whole system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you're changing your answers all the time. Earlier you said, "everyone in town knew, let alone the army," which means to the extent those in town would not have known, at least everyone in the army would have known. And now you're twisting it the other way around. I just make this observation so that you're aware of how your evidence at this moment is perceived. Please proceed, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: A moment ago --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You referred to logistics that would be required, engineering equipment that would be required, people needed to be transported, people needed to be secured, people needed to be guarded and so on and so forth. All of those activities would have had to have been coordinated centrally. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Somewhere at some level, whether at the level of the corps, because there was a cooperation between the corps. But as I said, at the beginning, I was not included in any planning for the operation and that I have nothing to do with it. Now, who had what role to play, that can be seen from the documents pertaining to the planning of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about what you knew, when you knew it. And so when you had your conversation with Miso Pelemis, commander of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, and he told you of the extent of the engagement of members of that unit in the massacres or the executions concerning Srebrenica, you believed that other members of the Main Staff were aware of this information, right? You've confirmed that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I believed it to be the case. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you believed that General Mladic knew about that information as well, which is why you didn't report it to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. This is a directly leading question outside the context of anything we touched upon in our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last is not exactly accurate, but the question certainly is leading, if you could rephrase it, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you believe that General Mladic knew about the crimes that you learned were committed by members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment as conveyed to you by the unit's commander, Pelemis?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Believe me. At that moment I didn't even think about it, whether he knew or not. I thought that the competent security organs knew by that time, and I thought it was a process that was going on for some time and I was surprised then, and I still feel the same way. Even today I find it difficult to comprehend that something like that was possible, and yet it happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you asked for what the witness believed. Could I ask you the following? Is there any fact to your knowledge that Mr. Mladic would not have known what you said everyone knew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not attend the briefings. I was away quite a lot, and excluded from it, so I can't assert anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have to assert anything whether he knew or not. I'm asking you whether there is any fact to your knowledge that Mr. Mladic would not have known. You said everyone in town, let alone the army, knew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not the army. Not -- well, most of the officers who were supposed to know probably did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm not asking you who knew and who did not know. I'm asking you is there any fact, to your knowledge, that Mr. Mladic would not have known what you described as was known to everyone in town, let alone in the army. Any fact. I'm only seeking facts, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have a fact. I can't provide it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Colonel, aside from your legal responsibilities concerning the information that you came into from Pelemis, it was your job, wasn't it, as the chief of intelligence, to relay important information, whatever information, to the commander of the Main Staff, whether that be through General Tolimir, your immediate superior, or directly, as you did when you spoke to him in Srebrenica on 13 July? Didn't you have a responsibility to relay this information to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did, yes. I did have an obligation to discuss it with Tolimir, and I think work was being done on gathering information in that regard. At least as far as I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're the chief of intelligence of the intelligence administration of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you're telling this Chamber that you think, not know, but you think that information regarding crimes of which you've testified previously and reiterated today that you were horrified about, that the scale was almost incomprehensible to you, you think information was being gathered concerning those crimes but you don't know?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SALAPURA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. What I'm saying is that the security service must have been gathering information and working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again intervene --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Checking the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please. Facts you are aware of which would have indicated that investigations were ongoing. That's what I'm asking for, not on whether it should have been the case or whether you -- it would be logical, but just facts indicating that the matter was investigated. If you have any, please tell us. If not, tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't. I didn't see anyone being interrogated or investigated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer is given, no. Next question, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me put a question to you, Mr. Salapura. Mr. Vanderpuye asked you just a couple of minutes ago: "Didn't you have a responsibility to relay this information to General Mladic?" You didn't answer that question. You answered in a different way. "I did have an obligation to discuss it with Tolimir." It was not the question of -- about an obligation to discuss but a question about the responsibility to report, to relay this information to the commander, General Mladic. Did you have that obligation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I discussed it with Tolimir. My superior. My superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question was very clear: Did you have, and I repeat that, the responsibility to relay this information to General Mladic? Which means to report, not to discuss, to report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to General Mladic. I had to speak with General Mladic, my superior.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: With General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I explain? I sent intelligence information to the -- to Mr. Mladic about the enemy, their plans, and what was going on, but this was an internal problem which had to do -- well, I told you I discussed it with Mr. Tolimir, and obviously, it was known by many people. So my job was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was about to go to a different area and I see that we are out of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We will adjourn for the day, and Mr. Salapura, I would again like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony already given or testimony still to be given, and we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may follow the usher.
